stimuli.title: Plant the Shade
stimuli.text:
Every summer, the same neighborhoods in our city break the same records. Bus stops turn into ovens. Sidewalks are too hot to touch. And every summer, the city council discusses the problem and does very little. It is time for a simple, proven solution: plant trees, and plant them where they are needed most.

A grown street tree is a remarkable machine. Its leaves block sunlight before it can heat the pavement, and they release water vapor that cools the air around them, much as sweat cools skin. People who measure city temperatures have found that a street shaded by trees can be several degrees cooler than a bare street only a few blocks away. Trees also soak up rainwater that would otherwise flood storm drains, and they make walking more pleasant, which means fewer short trips by car.

Critics say trees are expensive to plant and care for, and that their roots crack sidewalks. These concerns are real, but they are not reasons to do nothing. Choosing the right kind of tree for each street, and giving its roots enough room, prevents most sidewalk damage. As for cost, a tree's benefits grow every year it lives, while the cost of a heat wave, in hospital visits and electric bills, arrives all at once.

The neighborhoods that suffer most from heat are often the ones with the fewest trees. The council should start there, this year. Shade should not be a luxury.

stimuli.title: The Lamp Room
stimuli.text:
Mara had never been inside the lighthouse at night. All summer her grandfather had climbed the ninety-two steps alone each evening, a thermos of tea in one hand and a rag for the brass in the other, while she watched from the cottage window. "When you're older," he always said, and Mara had begun to suspect that older was a place she would never reach.

Then, on the last Friday of August, he stopped halfway up the porch steps and pressed a hand to his knee. "Well," he said, studying the sky, which had gone the color of a bruise, "I suppose tonight you are older."

The stairs wound so tightly that Mara could touch both walls at once. At the top, the lamp room smelled of oil and salt. Her grandfather lowered himself onto a stool and talked her through every step: trim the wick, wipe the lens, wind the clockwork that turned the light. His voice was calm, but she noticed that he never took his eyes off her hands.

When the beam finally swept out across the water, Mara pressed her face to the glass. Far out, a fishing boat was pushing toward the harbor, rising and dipping on the dark swells. She watched it until its lights slid safely behind the breakwater.

"They'll never know who lit it," she said.

Her grandfather smiled. "That," he said, "is exactly the point."

stimuli.title: In Defense of Bats
stimuli.text:
Few animals have a worse reputation than bats. In stories they are spooky and sneaky, and probably up to no good. But the real bats of North America deserve our protection, not our fear, and the reasons are practical as much as they are kind.

Consider insects. A single little brown bat can catch hundreds of small insects in an hour of hunting. Across a whole colony, over a whole summer, that adds up to tons of insects that never reach farm fields. Scientists who study crop pests estimate that bats save American farmers billions of dollars a year in pesticides they do not have to buy. Some bats in warmer regions do another job as well: they pollinate plants, carrying pollen from flower to flower as they feed on nectar.

Yet bats are in trouble. A disease called white-nose syndrome has killed millions of bats that spend the winter in caves. Wind turbines, though important for clean energy, kill many bats that fly into their blades. And because many bats raise only one pup a year, their numbers recover slowly.

There are simple ways to help. People can leave old trees standing where bats roost, put up bat houses, and stay out of caves that are closed to protect sleeping colonies. Wind farms can slow their blades on calm nights, when bats are most active. None of this requires us to love bats. It only requires us to notice how much they already do for us.

stimuli.title: Moving Day
stimuli.text:
The boxes stand like silent towers,

our whole house folded into squares.

My mother tapes the kitchen shut;

my father wrestles down the stairs

the couch we've sat on every winter,

its cushions shaped by all of us.

I carry out my own small carton

and do not make a fuss.

But at the door I turn around:

the rooms have grown too wide, too bare,

and on the wall, in pencil lines,

my heights climb up the closet there.

I cannot pack a pencil line.

I press my hand against the last,

the highest one, from just last June,

and promise I will grow up fast

in some new hallway, some new house,

where no one knows how tall I've been,

until I mark a brand-new wall

and start the climbing once again.

stimuli.title: More Than Books
stimuli.text:
When most people picture a public library, they imagine shelves of books and a librarian whispering "shh." But many libraries across the country now lend things that would surprise a visitor from fifty years ago: telescopes, sewing machines, ukuleles, cake pans shaped like dinosaurs, even power drills. Some people call these collections a distraction from a library's real job. I think they are the library's real job, brought up to date.

A library has always been a way for a community to share things that are too costly for most people to own alone. In the 1800s, books were expensive, so towns pooled their money and bought them for everyone. Today a family can buy a paperback for a few dollars, but a telescope or a set of tools may cost hundreds. A family that uses a drill twice a year should not have to buy one, and a child curious about the stars should not have to wait until her parents can afford a telescope.

Lending objects also brings in people who might never have walked through the door. A father who comes to borrow a ladder may leave with a stack of picture books for his kids. A teenager who borrows a guitar may stay for a free lesson in the meeting room.

Of course, books must stay at the heart of the library. But a library that shares only books is like a bakery that sells only one kind of bread. The idea behind it is bigger than its shelves.

stimuli.title: Nothing Tender
stimuli.text:
Theo planted his tomato seedlings on the first warm Saturday in April, ignoring the sign at the community garden gate that read, in Mrs. Okafor's careful capitals, NOTHING TENDER BEFORE MAY 10. Tender, he decided, was for lettuce. Tomatoes were tough. They had thick, hairy stems and smelled sharp and green when you brushed against them.

For a week the plants looked splendid. Then came a clear, still night, the kind that makes the stars look close enough to touch, and in the morning the leaves hung black and limp, as if someone had boiled them.

Theo was crouched over the ruined row when a shadow fell across the dirt. Mrs. Okafor did not say a word about the sign. She knelt, pinched a leaf between two fingers, and sighed.

"Frost finds the eager ones first," she said. "I lost a whole bed of peppers my first spring here. Planted them on my birthday because I couldn't wait." She stood, brushing off her knees. "I have extra seedlings in my cold frame. Come by on the tenth and we'll put them in together."

Theo walked home slowly. He had expected a lecture, and somehow the lack of one made him feel worse, and then, by the time he reached his street, a little better. On the calendar by the refrigerator, he drew a fat red circle around May 10.

stimuli.title: Give Us Back the Stars
stimuli.text:
Step outside on a clear night in most American cities and count the stars. You may get to a dozen. A few generations ago, the same sky would have shown thousands. The stars have not gone anywhere. We have simply drowned them in light, and I believe it is time to turn some of it off.

Light at night is not only a problem for stargazers. Many birds migrate in the dark and steer partly by the stars; brightly lit buildings confuse them, and many crash into lit windows. Newly hatched sea turtles find the ocean by heading toward the brighter horizon over the water, so beachfront lights can lead them inland instead. Even people may sleep worse when a streetlight shines through the curtains all night.

Fixing this does not mean living in darkness. Much outdoor lighting is wasted because it shines sideways and up, into the sky and into bedroom windows, instead of down onto the sidewalk where it is needed. Shielded fixtures aim light at the ground. Timers and motion sensors switch lights off when no one is around. Warmer, dimmer bulbs cause less glare. Several towns have already made changes like these and found that their streets are still safe, their electric bills are lower, and their residents can see the Milky Way again.

Our town should join them. We protect rivers and forests because they belong to everyone. The night sky belongs to everyone too.

stimuli.title: The Recipe Card
stimuli.text:
My grandmother's recipe for corn bread is written on an index card so stained with butter that the ink has turned the color of weak tea. Half the measurements are missing. Where the card should say how much sugar, it says only "enough." Where it should give an oven temperature, it says "hot, but not mean."

For years I thought the card was useless. I tried to follow it the summer I turned eleven, and my corn bread came out as flat and pale as a paper plate. I complained to my grandmother on the phone. She laughed so hard she had to put the phone down.

"The card isn't the recipe," she said when she came back. "The card is just to remind me of the recipe. The recipe is in my hands."

The next time she visited, I stood beside her at the counter and watched. She did not measure anything. She poured cornmeal until the mound looked right, cracked eggs with one hand, and tested the batter by letting it drip off a spoon. When I asked how she knew when to stop stirring, she shrugged. "It tells you."

I have made that corn bread perhaps a hundred times since. I still keep the card in a drawer, though I no longer read it. I understand now that some knowledge does not fit on paper. It has to pass from one pair of hands to another, slowly, at a kitchen counter, the way it came to her.

stimuli.title: Every Child a Swimmer
stimuli.text:
Every summer, news stories remind us how quickly a day at the lake or the pool can turn tragic. Drowning is one of the leading causes of accidental death for young children in the United States. Yet in many neighborhoods, swimming lessons are something families have to pay for, and many simply cannot. Our city should offer free swimming lessons to every child in second grade.

Swimming is not just a sport. It is a safety skill, like looking both ways before crossing the street. A child who can float, tread water, and swim a short distance to the edge has a much better chance of staying safe after an unexpected fall into deep water. Children who learn young also tend to feel at home in the water, which makes them less likely to panic.

Some will say this is the job of parents, not the city. But we already teach children other safety skills in school, from fire drills to bicycle safety. And many parents never learned to swim themselves, so they cannot teach their children. A free program would break that cycle.

The cost would be modest. The city already owns three public pools that sit nearly empty on weekday mornings during the school year. Using them for lessons would cost far less than building anything new. Second graders could ride the bus there with their classes, the way they already go on field trips.

Learning to swim should not depend on the size of a family's bank account.

stimuli.title: Look at the Mailbox
stimuli.text:
Dev had been trying to ride the bicycle for three days, and for three days the bicycle had been winning. Each time Priya let go of the seat, he wobbled, panicked, and steered straight into the hedge as if it were pulling him in.

"You're looking at the hedge," Priya told him on the fourth morning. "Bikes go where your eyes go. Look at the mailbox at the end of the street."

"The mailbox is too far," Dev said.

"That's why it works."

He climbed on, jaw tight. Priya held the seat and jogged beside him, the way their father had once jogged beside her. She could feel the exact moment the bike stopped needing her: a lightness, as though a kite string had gone slack in her hand. She let go. Dev did not notice. He was staring at the mailbox, pedaling hard, his elbows sticking out like wings.

He reached it, braked too sharply, and tipped gently onto the grass. When he sat up, he was grinning so widely that Priya could see the gap where his front tooth had been.

"Did you let go?" he shouted.

"Ages ago," she called back, and found, to her surprise, that her eyes were stinging.

stimuli.title: Give Old Buildings a New Job
stimuli.text:
When an old building stands empty, the quickest plan is usually to knock it down and start over. The quickest plan is not always the best one. Our town should make a habit of reusing its old buildings instead of tearing them down.

Old buildings tell a town's story in a way that a plaque never can. The brick mill by the river, for instance, shows how people here once earned their living. Its tall windows were built to let in daylight before electric lights were common. Walking past it, a child can see that history instead of reading about it.

Reusing a building can also be the less wasteful choice. Tearing down a building fills trucks with broken brick and concrete, and a new building needs new materials, each made and shipped using energy. When a sturdy old building is repaired and given a new job, much of that material and energy is saved.

Some towns have turned old mills into apartments, old fire stations into restaurants, and old schools into community centers. These buildings often become the places people love most, because they feel different from anything built last year.

Not every old building can be saved. Some are unsafe, and some would cost too much to repair. But before our town approves another demolition, it should ask a simple question: could this building do something new? Too often, no one asks.

stimuli.title: Frog Headquarters
stimuli.text:
On the attic floor, under a box of old tax papers, Leo found a map his grandfather had drawn as a boy. It showed their town the way it had been sixty years ago, in faded blue ink. There was the river, the same as now, and the stone bridge. But where the shopping center stood today, the map showed a pond labeled FROG HEADQUARTERS. Where Leo's school sat, it showed a field with a tiny drawing of a horse and the words OLD BESS, VERY GRUMPY.

Leo carried the map downstairs. His grandfather put on his reading glasses and was quiet for a long time.

"Bess bit me twice," he said finally. "Both times I deserved it."

That afternoon they walked the route on the map together. Most of the places were gone. The pond had been filled in, and the woods behind the church were now a row of tidy houses. Leo kept waiting for his grandfather to be sad, but instead he kept stopping to point. "The fort was right there. Your great-uncle fell out of that oak, broke his arm, and bragged about it all summer."

By the time they got home, Leo had decided to make a map of his own. He would put in the skate park, the corner store with the good slushies, and the yard with the barking dog. Someday, he thought, somebody might need to know.

questions.stem: What is 3/4 + 1/8?
questions.explanation: Write 3/4 as 6/8, then 6/8 + 1/8 = 7/8. Adding the tops and the bottoms (4/12) is the classic mistake: the denominators must match first.

questions.stem: If n + 9 = 23, what is the value of n?
questions.explanation: Undo the + 9 by subtracting 9 from both sides: n = 23 − 9 = 14. Adding 9 instead gives 32.

questions.stem: A rectangle is 9 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: Perimeter adds all four sides: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26 cm. 13 cm adds only two sides, and 36 cm is the area number.

questions.stem: What is 0.6 × 0.4?
questions.explanation: 6 × 4 = 24, and the two factors have two decimal places in all, so the product is 0.24. A product of two numbers less than 1 is smaller than both, which rules out 2.4.

questions.stem: What is the value of 3x + 4 when x = 5?
questions.explanation: 3x means 3 times x, so 3 × 5 + 4 = 15 + 4 = 19. Reading 3x as 35 gives 39, and adding 3 + 5 + 4 gives 12.

questions.stem: Two angles of a triangle measure 50° and 60°. What is the measure of the third angle?
questions.explanation: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°, so 180 − 50 − 60 = 70°. 110° is just 50 + 60.

questions.stem: What is 25% of 64?
questions.explanation: 25% is one quarter, and 64 ÷ 4 = 16. Half of 64 is 32, which would be 50%.

questions.stem: At an animal shelter, the ratio of cats to dogs is 3 to 5. There are 15 cats. How many dogs are there?
questions.explanation: 15 cats is 5 groups of 3, so there are 5 groups of 5 dogs: 25. 40 is the total number of animals, and 9 flips the ratio.

questions.stem: What is the area of a triangle with a base of 10 meters and a height of 6 meters?
questions.explanation: Area = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × 10 × 6 = 30 square meters. 60 forgets the 1/2, which gives the area of a rectangle.

questions.stem: Which of these numbers is prime?
questions.explanation: 31 has no factors except 1 and itself. 21 = 3 × 7, 27 = 3 × 9, 33 = 3 × 11 and 39 = 3 × 13, so each of those is divisible by 3.

questions.stem: What number comes next in the pattern 2, 5, 11, 23, ...?
questions.explanation: Each number is double the one before plus 1: 2 × 23 + 1 = 47. The gaps 3, 6, 12 double each time, so the next gap is 24, and 23 + 24 = 47.

questions.stem: The mean of four test scores is 85. Three of the scores are 80, 90 and 82. What is the fourth score?
questions.explanation: Four scores with a mean of 85 add up to 4 × 85 = 340. The three known scores add up to 252, so the fourth is 340 − 252 = 88.

questions.stem: What is the value of 18 − 6 ÷ 2 + 1?
questions.explanation: Divide first: 6 ÷ 2 = 3. Then work left to right: 18 − 3 = 15, and 15 + 1 = 16. Subtracting before dividing gives (18 − 6) ÷ 2 + 1 = 7.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The city should plant street trees.
Heat waves are getting worse each year.
Tree roots damage too many sidewalks.
The council has handled the heat well.
Cars are the main cause of summer heat.
questions.explanation: The author calls trees "a simple, proven solution" and ends by telling the council to start planting this year. Root damage is an objection the author answers, not the main idea.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how do leaves cool the air around them?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says leaves release water vapor that cools the air, much as sweat cools skin. Leaves block sunlight too, but that keeps the pavement from heating; it is not how they cool the air.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the third paragraph is to:
options: list the best kinds of trees
questions.explanation: It begins "Critics say" and then replies to their two worries, cost and cracked sidewalks.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the claim that trees cool city streets?
options: Trees soak up rain that floods drains.
Some tree roots crack the sidewalks.
Trees cost money to plant and keep.
questions.explanation: Temperature measurements comparing shaded and bare streets show the cooling directly. Soaking up rain is a real benefit, but it is about flooding, not heat.

questions.stem: In the last sentence, the word "luxury" most nearly means:
options: a thing only a few get
questions.explanation: The author has just said the hottest neighborhoods have the fewest trees, so shade should not belong only to the lucky few. A costly kind of tree mixes up luxury with price.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about:
options: a girl doing her grandfather's job
a storm that wrecks a fishing boat
how lighthouses were built long ago
a girl who is afraid of tall stairs
a grandfather who wants to retire
questions.explanation: The story follows Mara as she climbs the lighthouse and lights the lamp for the first time, the job her grandfather has always done. The boat reaches the harbor safely, so nothing is wrecked.

questions.stem: Why does the grandfather say, "I suppose tonight you are older"?
options: Mara has just had a birthday.
He wants to stay with the boat.
The lamp no longer needs care.
His knee is too sore to climb.
He is busy fixing the cottage.
questions.explanation: He stops on the steps and presses a hand to his knee just before he says it, so he needs Mara to do the climbing. Nothing in the story mentions a birthday.

questions.stem: The sky that "had gone the color of a bruise" was most likely:
questions.explanation: A bruise is dark purple and gray, and the grandfather studies the sky as if worried; a fishing boat later fights dark swells. A clear, bright sky would not need a keeper's attention.

questions.stem: While Mara does each step in the lamp room, her grandfather:
questions.explanation: The passage says he never took his eyes off her hands. The tea and the brass are part of his usual evenings, not what he does that night.

questions.stem: When the grandfather says, "That is exactly the point," he most likely means that:
options: the light should be kept secret
the work is for others, not praise
Mara should tell the boat's crew
questions.explanation: Mara notices the sailors will never know who lit the lamp, and her grandfather agrees that this is the point: the work keeps people safe whether or not anyone thanks the keeper.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Bats are more dangerous than people think.
Bats are useful and need our protection.
Wind farms should be shut down for good.
Most stories about bats are true.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says bats deserve "our protection, not our fear," and the rest explains what they do for us and how to help them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do bat numbers recover slowly?
options: They sleep in very cold caves.
They eat only one kind of insect.
They fly only on calm nights.
They avoid living in old trees.
Many have just one pup a year.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph links the slow recovery to raising only one pup a year. Cold caves are where bats spend the winter, not the reason numbers recover slowly.

questions.stem: The author's view of wind turbines is that they:
options: matter but should be run with care
are useless and should be removed
pose no danger to any wildlife
are more useful than bat houses
are the cause of white-nose syndrome
questions.explanation: The author calls turbines "important for clean energy" but notes they kill bats and suggests slowing the blades on calm nights. White-nose syndrome is a disease, not something turbines cause.

questions.stem: The author mentions the money farmers save on pesticides mainly to:
questions.explanation: The point comes right after the author says the reasons to protect bats are practical: bats eat crop pests, so farmers spend less.

questions.stem: The last two sentences suggest that the author believes people:
options: do too much to help animals
questions.explanation: "None of this requires us to love bats" means the steps work even for people who still find bats creepy; noticing their value is enough.

questions.stem: In the first stanza, the boxes are compared to:
questions.explanation: The first line says the boxes stand "like silent towers." Squares appear in the next line, but they describe the folded house, not what the boxes are compared to.

questions.stem: The pencil lines on the closet wall show:
options: a map of the new street
questions.explanation: The poem says "my heights climb up the closet there," so each line marks the speaker's height at a different time.

questions.stem: At the door, the speaker feels mostly:
options: sad to leave the old home
questions.explanation: The speaker turns back, notices the rooms are bare, and presses a hand against the height marks, all signs of missing the old house. The rooms seem too wide, but the speaker is not frightened of them.

questions.stem: The line "I cannot pack a pencil line" suggests that:
options: the speaker has run out of boxes
pencil marks are easy to erase
some memories have to stay behind
questions.explanation: The height marks stand for years of growing up in the house, and they have to stay behind on the wall. The line is about memories, not a shortage of boxes.

questions.stem: At the end of the poem, the speaker expects to:
options: move back to the old house
begin a new record of growing
stay the same height for years
questions.explanation: The last stanza imagines marking "a brand-new wall" and starting "the climbing once again," a new set of height lines in the new house.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as TIMID?
questions.explanation: Timid means easily frightened or shy, like a timid puppy hiding behind a chair. Loud is close to the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as VAST?
questions.explanation: Vast means very large in size or amount, as in a vast desert. A vast space may also be empty, but empty is not what the word means.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as ASSIST?
questions.explanation: To assist is to help, as when a nurse assists a doctor. Ask looks a little like assist but means something different.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as RAPID?
questions.explanation: Rapid means very fast, as in a rapid heartbeat, and swift also means fast. Steady describes an even pace, not a fast one.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as FRAGILE?
questions.explanation: Something fragile breaks easily, like a glass ornament, and delicate means the same. Heavy has nothing to do with breaking.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as RELUCTANT?
questions.explanation: A reluctant helper does not want to help: reluctant means unwilling. Unable is a trap: an unable person cannot do something, a reluctant one does not want to.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as ABUNDANT?
questions.explanation: Abundant means more than enough, as in an abundant harvest, so plentiful is the match. Rare is the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as CANDID?
questions.explanation: A candid answer is honest and direct, which is what frank means. Sweet is a trap from the look-alike word candy.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as DILIGENT?
questions.explanation: A diligent student works hard and steadily, and industrious means hardworking. Inattentive is nearly the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as SERENE?
questions.explanation: Serene means peaceful and calm, like a serene lake at dawn. Solemn means serious, which is not the same as peaceful.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as CONCEAL?
questions.explanation: To conceal something is to hide it. Reveal is the opposite, and seal only shares some letters.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as OBSOLETE?
questions.explanation: Obsolete means no longer used because something newer has replaced it, like a typewriter: outdated. An obsolete machine may still work, so broken is not the meaning.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as HOSTILE?
questions.explanation: Hostile means unfriendly or ready to fight, as in a hostile crowd. Generous is close to the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as METICULOUS?
questions.explanation: A meticulous person pays careful attention to every detail, so precise is closest. Meticulous work can take a long time, but lengthy is not the meaning.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as BENEVOLENT?
questions.explanation: Benevolent means kind and wanting to do good for others. A benevolent person may also be wealthy, but the word is about kindness.

questions.stem: Puppy is to dog as kitten is to:
questions.explanation: A puppy grows up to be a dog, and a kitten grows up to be a cat. A kitten may chase a mouse, but that is a different relationship.

questions.stem: Hot is to cold as tall is to:
questions.explanation: Hot and cold are opposites, and the opposite of tall is short. Higher only compares heights; it is not the opposite of tall.

questions.stem: Pen is to write as knife is to:
questions.explanation: A pen is used to write, and a knife is used to cut. Sharp describes the knife but is not what it is used for.

questions.stem: Glove is to hand as sock is to:
questions.explanation: A glove covers a hand, and a sock covers a foot. A shoe goes over the sock; it is not what the sock covers.

questions.stem: Page is to book as petal is to:
questions.explanation: A page is one part of a book, and a petal is one part of a flower. A stem is another part, not the whole.

questions.stem: Pilot is to airplane as captain is to:
questions.explanation: A pilot is in charge of flying an airplane, and a captain is in charge of a ship. A ship moves across the ocean, but the captain commands the ship.

questions.stem: Whisper is to shout as drizzle is to:
questions.explanation: A whisper is a very soft sound and a shout a very loud one; a drizzle is very light rain and a downpour very heavy rain. Mist is even lighter than drizzle, the wrong direction.

questions.stem: Library is to books as orchard is to:
questions.explanation: A library is a collection of books, and an orchard is a collection of planted fruit trees. A farmer works in an orchard but is not what it is made of.

questions.stem: Thermometer is to temperature as scale is to:
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature, and a scale measures weight. Height is measured with a ruler or tape, not a scale.

questions.stem: Author is to novel as composer is to:
questions.explanation: An author writes a novel, and a composer writes a symphony. An orchestra plays the symphony but is not what the composer creates.

questions.stem: Bark is to dog as:
questions.explanation: A bark is the sound a dog makes, and a neigh is the sound a horse makes. A cow gives milk, which is a product, not a sound.

questions.stem: Coward is to courage as liar is to:
questions.explanation: A coward lacks courage, and a liar lacks honesty. A liar does not tell the truth, but truth is a statement, while honesty is the quality the liar is missing, just as courage is.

questions.stem: Drought is to water as famine is to:
questions.explanation: A drought is a long lack of water, and a famine is a lack of food. Hunger is what a famine causes, not what it lacks.

questions.stem: Chapter is to book as:
questions.explanation: A chapter is one section of a book, and a scene is one section of a play. An actor works on a stage but is not a section of it.

questions.stem: Cautious is to careless as:
questions.explanation: Cautious and careless are opposites, and so are generous and stingy. Each of the other pairs is made of two words that mean nearly the same thing.

questions.stem: What is 2/3 of 45?
questions.explanation: One third of 45 is 15, so two thirds is 2 × 15 = 30. 15 is only one third, and 67.5 comes from multiplying by 3/2 instead of 2/3.

questions.stem: If 4y = 36, what is the value of y?
questions.explanation: Divide both sides by 4: y = 36 ÷ 4 = 9. 32 subtracts 4 instead of dividing, and 144 multiplies.

questions.stem: How many inches are in 3 1/2 feet?
questions.explanation: 1 foot is 12 inches, so 3 feet is 36 inches and half a foot is 6 more: 42. 36 leaves out the half foot.

questions.stem: A jacket that costs \$80 is on sale for 15% off. What is the sale price?
questions.explanation: 15% of \$80 is 0.15 × 80 = \$12, and \$80 − \$12 = \$68. \$12 is the amount saved, not the price, and \$92 adds the discount instead of taking it off.

questions.stem: A car travels at a steady 50 miles per hour. How far does it go in 3 1/2 hours?
questions.explanation: Distance = rate × time = 50 × 3.5 = 175 miles. 150 miles counts only the 3 whole hours.

questions.stem: What is the least common multiple of 6 and 8?
questions.explanation: Multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24, ... and 24 is the first one that 6 also divides. 48 is a common multiple but not the least, and 2 is the greatest common factor.

questions.stem: A cube has edges that are 3 inches long. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Volume = length × width × height = 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubic inches. 9 is the area of one face, and 54 is the total area of all six faces.

questions.stem: Which expression means "6 less than twice a number n"?
questions.explanation: Twice the number is 2n, and 6 less than that is 2n − 6. "Less than" reverses the order you read it, so 6 − 2n is a common trap; 2(n − 6) takes 6 away before doubling.

questions.stem: What is 4.5 ÷ 0.09?
questions.explanation: Multiply both numbers by 100 to clear the decimal in the divisor: 450 ÷ 9 = 50. Check: 50 × 0.09 = 4.5. The value 0.405 is what you get by multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A bag holds 4 red, 5 blue and 3 green marbles. One marble is picked without looking. What is the probability that it is blue?
questions.explanation: There are 4 + 5 + 3 = 12 marbles and 5 are blue, so the probability is 5/12. 5/7 compares blue with the 7 marbles that are not blue.

questions.stem: If 2x − 7 = 15, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Add 7 to both sides: 2x = 22. Divide by 2: x = 11. Subtracting 7 instead gives 2x = 8 and x = 4; stopping at 2x gives 22.
−7 + 12 = 5, and subtracting −3 is the same as adding 3, so 5 + 3 = 8. Treating − (−3) as − 3 gives 2.

questions.stem: What is 5/6 − 1/4?
questions.explanation: Use twelfths: 5/6 = 10/12 and 1/4 = 3/12, so 10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12. Subtracting tops and bottoms separately gives 4/2, which is not even close.

questions.stem: If m − 6 = 14, what is the value of m?
questions.explanation: Undo the − 6 by adding 6 to both sides: m = 14 + 6 = 20. Subtracting 6 again gives 8.

questions.stem: A square has a perimeter of 36 feet. How long is each side?
questions.explanation: A square has 4 equal sides, so each is 36 ÷ 4 = 9 feet. 6 feet is the side of a square with an area of 36.

questions.stem: What is 3,476.82 rounded to the nearest hundred?
questions.explanation: The hundreds digit is 4 and the digit after it is 7, so round up to 3,500. 3,480 is the nearest ten and 3,477 the nearest whole number.

questions.stem: What is the value of a² − b when a = 4 and b = 3?
questions.explanation: a² = 4 × 4 = 16, and 16 − 3 = 13. Reading a² as 2 × 4 = 8 gives 8 − 3 = 5.

questions.stem: A rug is 6 feet long and 4 feet wide. How many square feet of floor does it cover?
questions.explanation: Area = length × width = 6 × 4 = 24 square feet. 20 is the perimeter, the distance around the rug.
Line up the decimal points: 1.25 + 0.60 + 3.00 = 4.85. Lining up the last digits instead of the decimal points gives 1.34.

questions.stem: A pack of 6 juice boxes costs \$4.50. At this rate, how much do 10 juice boxes cost?
questions.explanation: One box costs \$4.50 ÷ 6 = \$0.75, so 10 boxes cost \$7.50. \$45.00 multiplies the pack price by 10 instead of the price of one box.

questions.stem: What is the median of the numbers 7, 3, 9, 4 and 15?
questions.explanation: Put them in order: 3, 4, 7, 9, 15. The middle number is 7. 9 is the middle of the list as written, before ordering, and 7.6 is the mean.

questions.stem: 30 is what percent of 120?
questions.explanation: 30 ÷ 120 = 0.25, which is 25%. 4% comes from dividing 120 by 30 and calling the answer a percent.

questions.stem: x is a whole number, and 4 < x + 2 < 7. Which of these could x be?
questions.explanation: Subtract 2 from each part: 2 < x < 5, so x can be 3 or 4. x = 2 makes x + 2 equal 4, which is not greater than 4, and x = 5 makes it 7, which is not less than 7.

questions.stem: Two angles together form a straight line. One of them measures 115°. What does the other measure?
questions.explanation: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°, so 180 − 115 = 65°. 245° is what you get using 360° instead.

questions.stem: Which expression has a value of 48?
questions.explanation: Parentheses first: 2 + 6 = 8, and 6 × 8 = 48. Without parentheses 6 × 2 + 6 is 12 + 6 = 18, and 3 + 5 × 8 is 3 + 40 = 43.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the author's main point?
options: Books cost too much to buy today.
questions.explanation: The author says lending telescopes and drills is "the library's real job, brought up to date," because libraries exist to share costly things. The author insists books stay at the heart of the library.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why did towns in the 1800s buy books for everyone?
options: Towns had too many old books.
Books were costly to buy alone.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says books were expensive then, so towns pooled their money. Today paperbacks are cheap, which is why the author turns to other costly items.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe the father who comes to borrow a ladder?
options: to show that ladders are popular
to show tools draw in new users
to argue fathers read too little
to explain how a loan is made
questions.explanation: The paragraph begins by saying lending objects brings in people who might never have come, and the father leaves with picture books, so the example shows that effect.

questions.stem: The comparison to a bakery that sells only one kind of bread suggests that a library:
options: is less useful than a bakery
costs too much money to run
can share many kinds of things
questions.explanation: A bakery with one bread would be offering far less than it could; the author means a library that lends only books is doing the same.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree with which statement?
options: Only books belong in a library.
Sharing costly things helps a town.
Telescopes are a waste of money.
Children should buy their own tools.
questions.explanation: The whole argument rests on the idea that a community gains by sharing things that are too costly for one family to own.

questions.stem: Which of these best tells what the passage is about?
options: A boy learns to be patient.
A gardener scolds a careless boy.
A boy builds his first cold frame.
A boy decides to quit gardening.
questions.explanation: Theo plants too early, loses his plants to frost, and ends by circling the safe planting date, so he has learned to wait. Mrs. Okafor never scolds him; the story says he expected a lecture and did not get one.

questions.stem: As it is used on the garden sign, the word "tender" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: The sign warns against planting before May 10, and the frost that kills Theo's tomatoes shows what it meant: plants that cold can damage. Theo thinks it means soft, like lettuce, and that is his mistake.

questions.stem: What happened to Theo's tomato plants?
questions.explanation: After a clear, still night the leaves were black and limp. "As if someone had boiled them" is a comparison, not what happened.

questions.stem: Mrs. Okafor most likely tells the story about her peppers in order to:
options: show she once did the same
questions.explanation: She lost her peppers by planting too early because she could not wait, just as Theo did, so the story tells him the mistake is a common one.

questions.stem: Why does Theo draw a circle around May 10 on the calendar?
options: The garden will close that day.
He will plant again that day.
He wants to remember the frost.
His tomatoes will be ripe then.
questions.explanation: Mrs. Okafor invites him to come on the tenth to plant her extra seedlings together, and May 10 is the date on the sign.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Cities have lost all of their stars.
The town should cut wasted light.
Sea turtles should stay off beaches.
questions.explanation: The author asks the town to aim, time and dim its lights as other towns have. The stars have not been lost; the author says they are hidden by light.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how do newly hatched sea turtles find the ocean?
options: by following their mothers to the water
by smelling the salt in the air
by listening for the crashing waves
by steering by the stars overhead
by heading toward the brighter horizon
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says hatchlings head for the brighter horizon over the water, which is why beach lights can lead them inland. Steering by the stars is what the passage says migrating birds do.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the second paragraph is to show that night lighting:
options: helps stars form in the sky
has been fixed in some towns
questions.explanation: It opens with "Light at night is not only a problem for stargazers" and gives birds, turtles and people as examples. The towns that fixed their lighting come in the third paragraph.

questions.stem: Which detail does the author offer as evidence that the changes can work?
options: Birds steer partly by the stars.
questions.explanation: Towns that shielded and timed their lights found their streets still safe and their bills lower, which shows the plan works. Warmer bulbs are one of the proposed changes, not the result of making them.

questions.stem: In the phrase "drowned them in light," the word "drowned" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: So much light floods the sky that the stars are hidden under it, so drowned here means hidden by too much of something. Soaked takes the word too literally; no water is involved.

questions.stem: The author's main point is that:
options: some skills are learned by doing
old index cards wear out quickly
the author no longer likes baking
questions.explanation: The essay ends by saying some knowledge does not fit on paper and must pass from one pair of hands to another: the author learned the recipe by watching and then making it, not by reading the card. The card was incomplete, not always wrong.

questions.stem: The card's words "hot, but not mean" suggest that the oven should be:
options: as hot as it will go
questions.explanation: "Hot" tells the baker to heat the oven well, and "not mean" says not to the point of burning. As hot as it will go is exactly what "not mean" rules out.

questions.stem: Why does the grandmother laugh when the author complains?
options: The card was never the full recipe.
The phone line was very noisy.
She had never baked corn bread.
She was glad the bread failed.
She wrote the card as a joke.
questions.explanation: She explains that the card only reminds her of a recipe that lives "in my hands," so following it word for word was never going to work.

questions.stem: How does the grandmother test the batter?
options: by tasting a small bite of it
by weighing it on a scale
by letting it drip off a spoon
by measuring how high it rises
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says she tested the batter by letting it drip off a spoon. She does not measure anything, so a scale is wrong.

questions.stem: The tone of the last paragraph is best described as:
questions.explanation: The author reflects calmly on what the grandmother passed on and keeps the card as a keepsake. The early complaint is gone by the end.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as GLEAM?
questions.explanation: To gleam is to shine with a soft or bright light, like a polished car. Glance starts the same way but means a quick look.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as FEEBLE?
questions.explanation: Feeble means weak, as in a feeble cry from a newborn kitten. None of the other words is about strength.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as ODOR?
questions.explanation: An odor is a smell, good or bad. The other words name different senses or features.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as VACANT?
questions.explanation: A vacant seat or lot has nothing or no one in it: it is empty. Crowded is the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as PERIL?
questions.explanation: Peril means serious danger, as in a ship in peril. A journey can be full of peril, but the words do not mean the same thing.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as ELATED?
questions.explanation: Elated means very happy and excited, so joyful is the match. Nervous describes a worried feeling, not a happy one.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as HUMBLE?
questions.explanation: A humble person does not boast about themselves, which is what modest means. Proud is the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as MEAGER?
questions.explanation: A meager meal is small and not enough, so skimpy is closest. Eager only sounds like meager, and plentiful is the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as PERSIST?
questions.explanation: To persist is to keep going even when it is hard, so continue is the match. Resist looks similar but means to fight against something.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as IMPARTIAL?
questions.explanation: An impartial judge does not take sides, so fair is the match. Incomplete is a trap: partial can mean part of something, but impartial means not favoring anyone.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as ARDUOUS?
questions.explanation: An arduous task takes great effort, like an arduous climb up a mountain: difficult. Ordinary does not suggest effort at all.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as TRANQUIL?
questions.explanation: Tranquil means quiet and peaceful, as in a tranquil garden. Stormy is the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as ADEQUATE?
questions.explanation: Adequate means good enough for what is needed, not more. Perfect goes too far, and equal only looks like part of the word.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as VERSATILE?
questions.explanation: A versatile tool or person can do many different things, so adaptable is the match. A versatile thing is often valuable, but that is not the meaning.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as SCRUTINIZE?
questions.explanation: To scrutinize something is to examine it very closely. Ignore is the opposite, and scribble only shares the opening sound.

questions.stem: Bird is to nest as bee is to:
questions.explanation: A bird lives in a nest, and a bee lives in a hive. Bees make honey, but honey is not their home.

questions.stem: Big is to large as small is to:
questions.explanation: Big and large mean the same, and so do small and little. Huge means the opposite of small.

questions.stem: Brush is to painter as hammer is to:
questions.explanation: A painter works with a brush, and a carpenter works with a hammer. A hammer hits a nail, but a nail is a thing, not the worker who uses the tool.

questions.stem: Doctor is to hospital as teacher is to:
questions.explanation: A doctor works in a hospital, and a teacher works in a school. A teacher teaches a student, but that is not the place.

questions.stem: Feather is to bird as scale is to:
questions.explanation: Feathers cover a bird's body, and scales cover a fish's body. Weight is a trap from the other meaning of scale, the one you stand on.

questions.stem: Cup is to drink as bowl is to:
questions.explanation: You use a cup to drink, and you use a bowl to eat from. A spoon goes with a bowl but is another object, not the action.

questions.stem: Freeze is to ice as melt is to:
questions.explanation: When water freezes, the result is ice; when ice melts, the result is water. Heat causes melting, but it is not what melting makes.

questions.stem: Seed is to tree as egg is to:
questions.explanation: A seed grows into a tree, and an egg hatches into a chicken. An eggshell and a yolk are parts of the egg, not what it becomes.

questions.stem: Ounce is to pound as:
questions.explanation: An ounce is a smaller unit of weight that makes up a pound, and an inch is a smaller unit of length that makes up a foot. Foot is to inch puts the two units the wrong way round.

questions.stem: Shy is to bashful as:
questions.explanation: Shy and bashful mean nearly the same thing, and so do glad and happy. Hot and cold are opposites.

questions.stem: Aquarium is to fish as:
questions.explanation: An aquarium is a place where fish are kept for people to see, and a zoo is a place where animals are kept for people to see. A tractor is a tool on a farm, not what the farm keeps on show.

questions.stem: Tiny is to enormous as quiet is to:
questions.explanation: Enormous is the far opposite end from tiny, and deafening is the far opposite end from quiet. Silent and whispering are on the same side as quiet.

questions.stem: Sculptor is to clay as weaver is to:
questions.explanation: A sculptor shapes clay, and a weaver works with yarn. A loom is the weaver's tool, not the material, and a rug is what the weaver makes.

questions.stem: Generous is to give as curious is to:
questions.explanation: A generous person likes to give, and a curious person likes to ask questions. Share goes with generous, not curious.

questions.stem: Novice is to expert as:
questions.explanation: A novice is a beginner and an expert is highly skilled; an apprentice is learning a trade and a master has mastered it. Friend and enemy are opposites, but not beginner and skilled.

questions.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 36 and 54?
questions.explanation: 36 = 2 × 18 and 54 = 3 × 18, and 2 and 3 share no factor, so 18 is the greatest. 6 and 9 are common factors but smaller; 108 is a common multiple.

questions.stem: Two numbers add up to 30, and one is 4 more than the other. What is the larger number?
questions.explanation: Take the 4 away and split the rest: (30 − 4) ÷ 2 = 13 is the smaller number, so the larger is 17. Check: 13 + 17 = 30.

questions.stem: On a coordinate grid, point A is at (2, 3) and point B is at (2, 9). How far apart are they?
questions.explanation: Both points have x = 2, so they lie on the same vertical line, and the distance is 9 − 3 = 6 units. 12 adds the y-values instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: A recipe uses 2 1/2 cups of flour for one batch. How many cups of flour are needed for 3 batches?
questions.explanation: 3 × 2 = 6 and 3 × 1/2 = 1 1/2, so 6 + 1 1/2 = 7 1/2 cups. Forgetting to multiply the half gives 6 1/2.

questions.stem: In a class of 30 students, the ratio of boys to girls is 2 to 3. How many girls are in the class?
questions.explanation: The ratio has 2 + 3 = 5 parts, so each part is 30 ÷ 5 = 6 students. Girls are 3 parts: 18. 12 is the number of boys.

questions.stem: What is the value of 3⁴?
questions.explanation: 3⁴ means 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81. 12 is 3 × 4, and 27 is only 3³.

questions.stem: How many minutes are in 2 1/4 hours?
questions.explanation: 2 hours is 120 minutes and a quarter hour is 15 minutes, so 135. 225 treats each hour as 100 minutes.

questions.stem: A plumber charges \$40 for a visit plus \$25 for each hour of work. Which expression gives the charge, in dollars, for h hours?
questions.explanation: The 40 is paid once and the 25 is paid for each hour, so the charge is 40 + 25h. 25 + 40h swaps the one-time fee and the hourly rate.

questions.stem: A \$40 game goes up in price by 10%, and then the new price goes down by 10%. What is the final price?
questions.explanation: Up 10%: 40 + 4 = \$44. Down 10% of \$44 is \$4.40, so \$44 − \$4.40 = \$39.60. The two changes do not cancel, because the second 10% is taken of a bigger number.

questions.stem: A circle has a radius of 5 cm. Using 3.14 for π, what is its circumference?
questions.explanation: Circumference = 2 × π × radius = 2 × 3.14 × 5 = 31.4 cm. 78.5 is the area (π × 5 × 5), and 15.7 forgets to double the radius.

questions.stem: What is the 10th number in the pattern 3, 7, 11, 15, ...?
questions.explanation: The pattern adds 4 each time. The 10th number is the 1st plus 9 jumps of 4: 3 + 36 = 39. 43 counts 10 jumps, and 35 is the 9th number.

questions.stem: What is 0.375 written as a fraction in lowest terms?
questions.explanation: 0.375 = 375/1000, and dividing top and bottom by 125 gives 3/8. 5/8 is 0.625, and 37/100 drops the last digit.

questions.stem: If 15 = k + 8, what is the value of k?
questions.explanation: Subtract 8 from both sides: k = 15 − 8 = 7. Check: 7 + 8 = 15.

questions.stem: How many sides does a hexagon have?
questions.explanation: A hexagon has 6 sides, like a honeycomb cell. A pentagon has 5 and an octagon has 8.

questions.stem: What is 7/10 written as a decimal?
questions.explanation: Seven tenths is 0.7, with the 7 in the tenths place. 0.07 is seven hundredths.

questions.stem: If p = 7, what is the value of 5p − 2?
questions.explanation: 5p = 5 × 7 = 35, and 35 − 2 = 33. Working 5 × (7 − 2) gives 25, which subtracts before multiplying.

questions.stem: What is the area of a square with sides 7 inches long?
questions.explanation: Area = side × side = 7 × 7 = 49 square inches. 28 is the perimeter.

questions.stem: What is 1/2 × 3/5?
questions.explanation: Multiply the tops and the bottoms: 1 × 3 = 3 and 2 × 5 = 10, so 3/10. Adding them instead gives 4/7.

questions.stem: Which equation says "a number n divided by 4 is 9"?
questions.explanation: The number n is the one being divided, so it comes first: n ÷ 4 = 9. 4 ÷ n divides 4 by the number instead.

questions.stem: What is the measure of each angle in an equilateral triangle?
questions.explanation: All three angles are equal and add up to 180°, so each is 180 ÷ 3 = 60°. 180° is the total, not one angle.

questions.stem: What is 12 × 15?
A train goes 240 miles in 4 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time = 240 ÷ 4 = 60 miles per hour. 960 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem: The high temperatures for five days were 62, 65, 70, 65 and 68 degrees. What is the mode?
questions.explanation: The mode is the value that appears most often, and 65 appears twice. 66 is the mean and 68 is the highest but one.

questions.stem: What is 10% of 350?
questions.explanation: 10% is one tenth, and 350 ÷ 10 = 35. 315 is what is left after taking 10% away.

questions.stem: Which value of n makes 7 × n = 84 true?
How many centimeters are in 4.5 meters?
questions.explanation: 1 meter is 100 centimeters, so 4.5 × 100 = 450. 4,500 uses 1,000, the number of millimeters in a meter.

questions.stem: What is 2.4 × 100?
questions.explanation: Multiplying by 100 moves each digit two places to the left, so 2.4 becomes 240. 24 is only 2.4 × 10.

questions.stem: What number comes next in the pattern 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...?
questions.explanation: These are square numbers: 1², 2², 3², 4², 5², so the next is 6² = 36. The gaps grow by 2 each time (3, 5, 7, 9), so the next gap is 11.

questions.stem: Ana's quiz scores were 7, 9, 10 and 6. What is the mean of her scores?
questions.explanation: Add the scores (7 + 9 + 10 + 6 = 32) and divide by how many there are: 32 ÷ 4 = 8. 4 is the range, 10 − 6.

questions.stem: A store sells 3 pens for \$1.20. At that price, what does 1 pen cost?
questions.explanation: \$1.20 ÷ 3 = \$0.40. \$3.60 is what 9 pens would cost, from multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A recipe needs 3 eggs to serve 4 people. How many eggs are needed to serve 12 people?
questions.explanation: 12 people is 3 times as many as 4, so the eggs triple: 3 × 3 = 9. 11 adds the 8 extra people to the 3 eggs.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides of 5 inches, 7 inches and 9 inches. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: Perimeter is the sum of the sides: 5 + 7 + 9 = 21 inches. 315 multiplies the sides.

questions.stem: What is 3/4 ÷ 1/2?
questions.explanation: Dividing by 1/2 is the same as multiplying by 2: 3/4 × 2 = 6/4 = 1 1/2. Multiplying by 1/2 instead gives 3/8.

questions.stem: Juan reads 24 pages in 40 minutes. At this rate, how many pages does he read in 1 hour?
questions.explanation: 24 pages in 40 minutes is 6 pages every 10 minutes, and an hour is 60 minutes, so 6 × 6 = 36 pages. 48 doubles the 24 as if 40 minutes were half an hour.

questions.stem: A box is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 2 cm tall. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Volume = 5 × 4 × 2 = 40 cubic centimeters. 11 adds the three lengths, and 76 is the surface area.

questions.stem: What is the value of 20 − 2 × (3 + 4)?
questions.explanation: Parentheses: 3 + 4 = 7. Multiply: 2 × 7 = 14. Subtract: 20 − 14 = 6. Working left to right without the rules gives (20 − 2) × 7 = 126.

questions.stem: On a map, 1 inch stands for 20 miles. Two towns are 3 1/2 inches apart on the map. How many miles apart are they?
questions.explanation: Each inch is 20 miles, so 3.5 × 20 = 70 miles. 60 miles counts only the 3 whole inches, and 23.5 adds the numbers.

questions.stem: A rectangle has an area of 54 square feet and a width of 6 feet. What is its length?
questions.explanation: Area = length × width, so length = 54 ÷ 6 = 9 feet. 21 feet treats 54 as the perimeter.

questions.stem: Which number is divisible by both 3 and 4?
questions.explanation: 132: its digits add to 6, so 3 divides it, and its last two digits, 32, are a multiple of 4. 124 passes the test for 4 but not 3; 126 passes for 3 but not 4.

questions.stem: What is the value of 2a + 3b when a = 5 and b = 4?
questions.explanation: 2a = 10 and 3b = 12, and 10 + 12 = 22. Adding all the numbers, 2 + 5 + 3 + 4, gives 14.

questions.stem: Three angles of a four-sided figure measure 90°, 90° and 120°. What does the fourth angle measure?
questions.explanation: The angles of any four-sided figure add up to 360°, and 90 + 90 + 120 = 300, so the fourth is 60°. A triangle's 180° total does not apply to four sides.

questions.stem: What is 60% of 45?
questions.explanation: 10% of 45 is 4.5, so 60% is 6 × 4.5 = 27. 18 is 40%, the part that is left over.

questions.stem: A paint color is mixed 2 parts blue to 5 parts white. How many cups of blue are needed for 20 cups of white?
questions.explanation: 20 cups of white is 4 groups of 5, so it needs 4 groups of 2 cups of blue: 8. 50 flips the ratio.

questions.stem: A spinner has 8 equal parts numbered 1 to 8. What is the probability of spinning a number greater than 5?
questions.explanation: Only 6, 7 and 8 are greater than 5, so 3 of the 8 equal parts: 3/8. 5/8 counts the numbers from 1 to 5 instead.

questions.stem: What is 5 − 8 + 2?
questions.explanation: Left to right: 5 − 8 = −3, and −3 + 2 = −1. Doing 8 + 2 first gives 5 − 10 = −5, which breaks the left-to-right rule.

questions.stem: Tickets cost \$6 each, and there is one \$3 booking fee for the whole order. Which expression gives the cost, in dollars, of t tickets?
questions.explanation: Each ticket costs 6, so t tickets cost 6t, and the fee is added once: 6t + 3. 9t would charge the fee on every ticket.

questions.stem: A parallelogram has a base of 12 meters and a height of 5 meters. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area = base × height = 12 × 5 = 60 square meters. 30 uses the triangle rule, which has a 1/2.

questions.stem: Which fraction is greater than 3/5?
questions.explanation: As decimals, 3/5 = 0.6 and 5/8 = 0.625, so 5/8 is greater. 7/12 is about 0.583 and 4/7 about 0.571, both a little less than 0.6.

questions.stem: Sam is 3 years older than Lee, and their ages add up to 27. How old is Sam?
questions.explanation: Take away the 3-year difference: 27 − 3 = 24, split evenly is 12 for Lee, so Sam is 15. 12 is Lee's age, not Sam's.

questions.stem: The minute hand of a clock turns from the 12 to the 3. How many degrees does it turn?
questions.explanation: A full turn is 360°, and 12 to 3 is a quarter of the clock face: 360 ÷ 4 = 90°. 30° is the turn from one number to the next.

questions.stem: Kim buys 2.5 pounds of apples at \$1.80 a pound. How much does she pay?
questions.explanation: 2.5 × 1.80 = 2 × 1.80 + 0.5 × 1.80 = 3.60 + 0.90 = \$4.50. \$4.30 adds the two numbers instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: If 3(x + 2) = 24, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Divide both sides by 3: x + 2 = 8. Subtract 2: x = 6. Stopping at 8 forgets the + 2.

questions.stem: A pool is 20 meters long, 10 meters wide and 2 meters deep. How many cubic meters of water does it hold when full?
questions.explanation: Volume = 20 × 10 × 2 = 400 cubic meters. 200 leaves out the depth, and 32 adds the three lengths.

questions.stem: What is the value of 4² + 3³?
questions.explanation: 4² = 16 and 3³ = 27, and 16 + 27 = 43. Multiplying the base by the exponent (8 + 9) gives 17.

questions.stem: If 5n − 3 = 2n + 9, what is the value of n?
questions.explanation: Subtract 2n from both sides: 3n − 3 = 9. Add 3: 3n = 12. Divide by 3: n = 4. Check: 5 × 4 − 3 = 17 and 2 × 4 + 9 = 17.

questions.stem: A rectangle 10 units long and 6 units wide has a square, 2 units on each side, cut out of one corner. What is the area of the shape that is left?
questions.explanation: The whole rectangle is 10 × 6 = 60 square units and the square removed is 2 × 2 = 4, so 60 − 4 = 56. 52 takes away 8, the square's perimeter, instead of its area.

questions.stem: A school has 480 students, and 35% of them walk to school. How many students walk?
questions.explanation: 10% of 480 is 48, so 35% is 3.5 × 48 = 168. 312 is the 65% who do not walk, and 144 is only 30%.

questions.stem: Gina has \$40 and saves \$15 more each week. After how many weeks will she have \$130?
questions.explanation: She needs \$130 − \$40 = \$90 more, and \$90 ÷ \$15 = 6 weeks. Dividing the whole \$130 by 15 gives about 8.7, which forgets the \$40 she already has.

questions.stem: Point P is at (4, −2) on a coordinate grid. Where is point P?
questions.explanation: x = 4 is to the right of the y-axis and y = −2 is below the x-axis, and right-and-below is Quadrant IV. Quadrant II is left-and-above.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The city should give free swim lessons.
Parents should teach their own children.
Public pools should close during school.
Swimming is the best sport for children.
Field trips should go to the lake.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph ends with the proposal, free lessons for every second grader, and the rest of the passage gives reasons and answers an objection.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when do the city's pools sit nearly empty?
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the three pools sit nearly empty on weekday mornings during the school year, which is when the lessons would happen.

questions.stem: Which detail does the author use to show that the plan would not cost much?
options: Children can learn to tread water.
The city already owns three pools.
Many parents never learned to swim.
questions.explanation: Using pools the city already owns would cost far less than building new ones. The other details support other parts of the argument.

questions.stem: The author compares swimming to looking both ways before crossing the street in order to:
options: show swimming is a safety skill
questions.explanation: The comparison comes right after "Swimming is not just a sport," so it presents swimming as a basic skill for staying safe.

questions.stem: How does the author answer people who say teaching swimming is the parents' job?
options: Parents spend too much on lessons now.
The city has more money than parents.
Children learn best from their friends.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph points out that schools already teach fire and bicycle safety, and adds that many parents cannot swim themselves.

questions.stem: Why does Priya tell Dev to look at the mailbox?
options: so he steers away from the hedge
so he can check for the mail
because the hedge has sharp thorns
so he can count how far he rode
questions.explanation: Priya says "Bikes go where your eyes go." Dev kept riding into the hedge because he was looking at it, so she gives him somewhere better to look.

questions.stem: The comparison to a kite string that "had gone slack" shows that Priya:
options: was tired from all the jogging
felt the bike balance on its own
questions.explanation: A slack string means nothing is pulling on it. Priya feels the bike stop needing her support, and right after that she lets go on purpose.

questions.stem: Who once helped Priya learn to ride a bike?
questions.explanation: She jogs beside Dev "the way their father had once jogged beside her."

questions.stem: Priya's eyes most likely sting at the end because she:
options: is upset that he fell over
is angry he did not thank her
is worried he will crash again
has been in the sun too long
questions.explanation: Dev rides all the way to the mailbox and grins, and Priya is surprised to find herself close to tears: she is touched, the way her father may once have been. The fall onto the grass is gentle and he is fine.

questions.stem: The statement that "the bicycle had been winning" means that:
options: the bike was much too fast
questions.explanation: For three days Dev could not stay on the bike, so the author jokes that the bicycle was winning a contest against him.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Every old building must be saved.
The mill should become a museum.
Towns should build more brick mills.
questions.explanation: The author asks the town to make reuse a habit but admits that not every old building can be saved, so "every" goes too far.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does the mill have tall windows?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the tall windows were built to let in daylight before electric lights were common.

questions.stem: The third paragraph mainly shows that reusing a building:
questions.explanation: It compares the broken brick and new materials of tearing down with the material and energy saved by repairing a sturdy old building.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward tearing down old buildings is best described as:
options: angry and refusing all of it
questions.explanation: The author argues for reuse but admits some buildings are unsafe or too costly to repair, and asks only that the town consider reuse first.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the idea that reused buildings are popular?
options: Tearing down fills trucks with brick.
The mill shows how people worked.
They often become places people love.
A plaque cannot tell a story.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says reused mills, fire stations and schools often become the places people love most. The other details support different points.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about:
options: a grandfather who hates how towns change
a map that shows a boy his town's past
how to draw a map that is accurate
a search for a horse that ran away
a family moving to a different town
questions.explanation: Leo finds his grandfather's old map, they walk its route together, and Leo learns what the town used to be. The grandfather is not sad; he keeps stopping to point.

questions.stem: What stands today where the frog pond used to be?
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the map shows the pond where the shopping center stands today. Leo's school is on the old field.

questions.stem: Leo expects his grandfather to be sad on the walk because:
options: most of the places are gone
the horse bit him two times
the old map has faded badly
the walk is long and tiring
questions.explanation: Most of the places on the map had been filled in or built over, so Leo thinks seeing them gone will make his grandfather sad.

questions.stem: In the phrase "a row of tidy houses," the word "tidy" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: Tidy means neat and in good order. Tiny sounds a little like it but means very small.

questions.stem: Leo's own map will most likely show:
options: only the main streets of town
the pond and the old field
places that matter to him now
questions.explanation: Leo plans to include the skate park, the corner store and the yard with the barking dog, the places in his own life, so that someone in the future will know them.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as PREDICT?
questions.explanation: To predict is to say what will happen before it does: to foretell. Prevent also starts with pre- but means to stop something from happening.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as CURIOUS?
questions.explanation: A curious person wants to know and find things out, so inquiring is the match. Furious rhymes with curious but means very angry.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as DEPART?
questions.explanation: To depart is to leave, as a train departs from a station. Arrive is the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as OPTIMISTIC?
questions.explanation: An optimistic person expects things to turn out well: hopeful. Doubtful is close to the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word means most nearly the same as FRIGID?
questions.explanation: Frigid means very cold, so icy is the match. A frigid greeting is also cold and unfriendly, but distant is a weaker idea and not the main meaning.

questions.stem: Hungry is to eat as tired is to:
questions.explanation: When you are hungry you eat, and when you are tired you sleep. Working and exercise make you more tired, not less.

questions.stem: Bread is to bakery as medicine is to:
questions.explanation: Bread is sold at a bakery, and medicine is sold at a pharmacy. A doctor writes a prescription, but neither is a store.

questions.stem: Fork is to utensil as oak is to:
questions.explanation: A fork is one kind of utensil, and an oak is one kind of tree. An acorn is the oak's seed, not the group it belongs to.

questions.stem: Mile is to distance as hour is to:
questions.explanation: A mile is a unit for measuring distance, and an hour is a unit for measuring time. A minute is another unit of time, not what is measured.

questions.stem: Flock is to sheep as:
questions.explanation: A flock is a group of sheep, and a pack is a group of wolves. A barn is where cows are kept, not a word for a group of them.
